meta.name: RPSGT Scoring Context Skill Cases
meta.copyrightBoundary: Original Sleep Pathways Guild teaching cases only. No patient recording, AASM scoring-manual figure, BRPT examination item, ISR item, or textbook figure is reproduced.
meta.clinicalBoundary: AASM Scoring Manual Version 3 is the governing scoring authority for rule-sensitive decisions in this pack. Atlas material is used only to validate physiologic appearance and context. AASM ISR interface behavior is not used as a substitute for the scoring rule itself.
suggestedStudyMaterials: Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al., for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.
Gupta, R., Pandi-Perumal, S. R., & BaHammam, A. S. (2018). Clinical atlas of polysomnography. Apple Academic Press.
Geyer, J. D., Carney, P. R., & Payne, T. A. (2010). Atlas of polysomnography (2nd ed.). Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

cases.title: Abrupt EEG shift after stable N2 sleep
cases.authority: AASM Version 3, Section V: Arousal Rules
cases.visualValidation: Atlas-style arousal morphology used only as visual corroboration; original SPG schematic.
cases.prompt: The schematic shows stable N2 sleep followed by an abrupt EEG frequency shift lasting about 4 seconds. What is the intended scoring decision?
options: Score an arousal
Do not score an arousal
Score a limb movement
Treat the EEG shift as artifact
cases.rationale: Version 3 requires an abrupt qualifying EEG-frequency shift lasting at least 3 seconds with at least 10 seconds of stable sleep before the change. This teaching trace supplies that N2 context. A modest chin-EMG rise is shown as supportive physiology, but a chin rise is not required for an NREM arousal.

evidence.label: The EEG changes abruptly for at least 3 seconds.
evidence.hint: Look for the clear change in EEG frequency near the end of the epoch. It should remain readable rather than looking like a dense artifact burst.

evidence.label: At least 10 seconds of stable sleep precedes the EEG change.
evidence.hint: Use the quiet N2 segment before the EEG shift as context.

evidence.label: A chin EMG increase is required for every arousal in every stage.
evidence.hint: Version 3 adds the concurrent chin-EMG requirement for stage R arousals, not for NREM arousals.

evidence.label: A respiratory event must be present before any arousal can be scored.
evidence.hint: The arousal rule does not require a preceding respiratory event.

cases.title: REM EEG shift without a chin increase
cases.authority: AASM Version 3, Section V: Arousal Rules
cases.visualValidation: Low REM chin tone and REM-style EEG/EOG context are original SPG teaching signals visually corroborated with atlas examples.
cases.prompt: During a schematic REM epoch, the EEG shifts abruptly for about 4 seconds but chin EMG does not increase. What is the intended decision?
options: Do not score an arousal
Score an arousal
Score a periodic limb movement
Score wake for the entire epoch
cases.rationale: Under AASM Scoring Manual Version 3, an arousal during stage R requires the qualifying EEG change plus a concurrent increase in submental EMG lasting at least 1 second. The EEG shift is present here, but the required concurrent chin-EMG increase is intentionally absent.

evidence.label: The surrounding epoch is REM sleep.
evidence.hint: Use the low chin tone and REM-style background as stage context.

evidence.label: There is no concurrent increase in chin EMG during the EEG shift.
evidence.hint: Compare the chin row directly under the EEG shift.

evidence.label: Any qualifying EEG frequency change is sufficient in REM even without a concurrent chin change.
evidence.hint: Version 3 requires a concurrent submental-EMG increase for an arousal in stage R.

evidence.label: Rapid eye movements automatically make an EEG shift an arousal.
evidence.hint: Eye movements help establish REM context but do not replace the arousal requirements.

cases.title: Repeating leg-EMG bursts during sleep
cases.authority: AASM Version 3, Section VII: Movement Rules
cases.visualValidation: Original SPG bilateral leg-EMG teaching pattern; atlas material is used only for physiologic appearance.
cases.prompt: The longer context view shows four discrete leg-EMG bursts during sleep, separated by roughly 20 seconds and not linked to respiratory events. What is the intended decision?
options: Score the movements as part of a periodic limb-movement series
Do not score any limb movements
Score the bursts as respiratory events
Treat every burst as electrical artifact
cases.answer: Score the movements as part of a periodic limb-movement series
cases.rationale: Version 3 defines a PLMS series using at least four consecutive leg movements with onset-to-onset intervals of 5–90 seconds. This teaching pattern supplies four discrete movements about 20 seconds apart during sleep and keeps them away from respiratory-event association.

evidence.label: Four discrete limb movements are present in the series.
evidence.hint: Count the separated leg-EMG bursts across the longer view.

evidence.label: The onset-to-onset spacing is about 20 seconds, within the Version 3 PLMS-series interval range.
evidence.hint: Compare the burst onsets: the movements are neither less than 5 seconds apart nor more than 90 seconds apart.

evidence.label: The entire displayed interval is wake, so the movements should be excluded.
evidence.hint: The schematic is explicitly presented as N2 sleep context.

evidence.label: Each leg burst occurs during a respiratory event.
evidence.hint: The airflow row remains stable around these movements.

cases.title: Leg bursts tied to respiratory events
cases.authority: AASM Version 3, Section VII: Movement Rules
cases.visualValidation: Original SPG leg-EMG and airflow timing schematic; atlas material is used only for visual corroboration.
cases.prompt: Several leg-EMG bursts occur during or immediately adjacent to the displayed respiratory events. How should those respiratory-linked movements be treated in this teaching case?
options: Do not count the respiratory-linked movements as periodic limb movements
Count every leg burst as a periodic limb movement
Score all leg bursts as arousals
Ignore the respiratory channels
cases.answer: Do not count the respiratory-linked movements as periodic limb movements
cases.rationale: Version 3 movement scoring includes respiratory-event timing as an exclusion when deciding whether a candidate leg movement contributes to PLMS scoring. The teaching schematic intentionally places the leg bursts at the respiratory-event terminations, so the respiratory association must be considered before counting a PLMS series.

evidence.label: The leg-EMG bursts occur at the displayed respiratory-event terminations.
evidence.hint: Compare the timing of each leg burst with the airflow reduction and recovery.

evidence.label: Respiratory-event timing changes whether these candidate leg movements count toward PLMS scoring.
evidence.hint: Do not decide from leg amplitude or series count alone; use the respiratory timing context.

evidence.label: Four visible leg bursts must always be counted as PLMS regardless of respiratory timing.
evidence.hint: Series count alone does not override the respiratory-event exclusion rule.

evidence.label: A chin EMG increase is the deciding requirement for periodic limb-movement scoring.
evidence.hint: Chin EMG is not the key exclusion demonstrated in this case.

cases.title: Single-channel abrupt transient
cases.authority: AASM Version 3 technical signal-validity principles; scoring decision remains conservative when signal origin is questionable.
cases.visualValidation: Clinical Atlas of Polysomnography, Chapter 12, and Geyer et al., artifact examples are used only to validate the original SPG artifact morphology.
cases.prompt: A large abrupt transient is concentrated in F3-M2 while neighboring derivations remain comparatively stable. What is the safest scoring interpretation?
options: Artifact / technical signal rather than a physiologic EEG event
Definite cortical arousal
Normal sleep spindle
Periodic limb movement
cases.answer: Artifact / technical signal rather than a physiologic EEG event
cases.rationale: A highly localized, nonphysiologic transient that is not corroborated in neighboring cerebral derivations should trigger signal-pathway and electrode-contact reasoning before it is accepted as cerebral scoring evidence.

evidence.label: The largest transient is isolated mainly to one EEG derivation.
evidence.hint: Compare F3-M2 with the neighboring EEG channels.

evidence.label: Neighboring channels do not show a convincing matching physiologic event.
evidence.hint: Physiologic interpretation should fit the cross-channel context.

evidence.label: Every EEG channel shows the same morphology at the same time.
evidence.hint: The defining clue is the opposite: the abnormal transient is highly localized.

evidence.label: A repeating leg-EMG series explains the transient.
evidence.hint: This case is localized to an EEG derivation rather than a leg-EMG pattern.

cases.title: Broad movement contamination
cases.authority: AASM Version 3 technical signal-validity principles; do not score obscured nonphysiologic activity as clean cerebral evidence.
cases.visualValidation: Clinical Atlas of Polysomnography, Chapter 12, and Geyer et al., artifact examples are used only to validate the original SPG movement-artifact morphology.
cases.prompt: A large irregular burst appears across EEG and EOG channels with increased chin activity over the same interval. What is the best overall interpretation?
options: Movement artifact affecting multiple channels
Isolated cortical arousal only
Single-electrode pop
Normal sleep spindle
cases.rationale: Broad simultaneous irregular contamination across multiple EEG/EOG channels with a concurrent EMG increase is a cross-channel movement pattern. It should not be presented to learners as a clean isolated cortical feature.

evidence.label: The irregular burst appears across several EEG/EOG channels at the same time.
evidence.hint: Follow the timing vertically across the montage.

evidence.label: Chin activity increases during the same contaminated interval.
evidence.hint: The EMG row supports a movement-related source.

evidence.label: Only one electrode is affected while all other channels remain clean.
evidence.hint: This tracing shows broad rather than isolated contamination.

evidence.label: The activity is a clean organized spindle confined to central EEG.
evidence.hint: The pattern is irregular and widespread rather than organized cerebral spindle activity.

cases.title: Arousal immediately before awakening
cases.authority: AASM Version 3, Section V: Arousal Rules
cases.visualValidation: Original SPG sleep-to-arousal-to-wake sequence; atlas material is used only for physiologic appearance.
cases.prompt: An abrupt qualifying EEG arousal begins late in an N2 epoch and is immediately followed by a transition to wake. Does the subsequent awakening erase the arousal?
options: No — score the arousal if its criteria are met
Yes — any transition to wake cancels the arousal
Score only a limb movement
Ignore the late-epoch event
cases.answer: No — score the arousal if its criteria are met
cases.rationale: AASM Scoring Manual Version 3 explicitly states that an arousal is scored when it immediately precedes a transition to stage W; both the arousal and the transition to wake are scored. The later wake transition therefore does not erase an otherwise qualifying arousal.

evidence.label: The qualifying EEG change begins while the preceding context is sleep.
evidence.hint: Focus on where the arousal begins, not only on what follows it.

evidence.label: Wake follows the arousal rather than replacing the preceding sleep context.
evidence.hint: The sequence is stable sleep → arousal → awakening.

evidence.label: Any wake activity after an arousal automatically cancels the arousal score.
evidence.hint: Version 3 explicitly permits scoring an arousal that immediately precedes transition to stage W.

evidence.label: Events near the end of an epoch should be ignored because another epoch follows.
evidence.hint: Epoch boundaries organize staging; they do not erase a qualifying arousal.

cases.title: Obstructive apnea crossing an epoch boundary
cases.authority: AASM Version 3, Section VIII Part 1: Adult Respiratory Rules
cases.visualValidation: Original SPG obstructive-apnea schematic; respiratory continuity and effort relationships are visually corroborated against atlas examples without copying them.
cases.prompt: In this adult diagnostic PSG, airflow falls to less than 10% of baseline for about 13 seconds while thoracic and abdominal effort continue. The event begins near the end of one 30-second epoch and continues into the next. What should be scored?
options: One obstructive apnea spanning the epoch boundary
Two obstructive apneas, one in each epoch
One central apnea spanning the epoch boundary
Do not score the event because it crosses an epoch boundary
cases.answer: One obstructive apnea spanning the epoch boundary
cases.rationale: AASM Scoring Manual Version 3 defines an adult apnea by a drop of at least 90% in the recommended apnea signal for at least 10 seconds. Continued or increased inspiratory effort throughout the absent-airflow period identifies an obstructive apnea. The epoch boundary does not divide one continuous respiratory event into two events.

evidence.label: The thermistor airflow signal falls by at least 90% from baseline during the event.
evidence.hint: For an adult diagnostic apnea, judge the airflow reduction using the oronasal thermal signal. The tracing becomes nearly flat during the event.

evidence.label: The reduction lasts about 13 seconds and inspiratory effort continues throughout it.
evidence.hint: Follow the thorax and abdomen channels while timing the near-flat thermal airflow segment across the boundary.

evidence.label: Crossing the 30-second boundary automatically turns one continuous event into two apneas.
evidence.hint: Measure the respiratory event continuously from onset until breathing returns toward baseline; the epoch line does not restart the event.

evidence.label: Continued thoracic and abdominal effort makes this a central apnea.
evidence.hint: A central apnea requires absent inspiratory effort; persistent effort supports obstruction.
